Fix d and N. First, the logarithmic derivatives used in C are regular at 1 after the stated pole removal. To see this for any modulus K, a nonprincipal character has bounded partial sums, so summation by parts continues its Dirichlet series holomorphically to Re s>0. The principal L-function is ζ(s) times the finite factors for primes dividing K. Subtracting the integral of v^(−s) on [1,∞) from the zeta series continues ζ(s) to Re s>0 with a simple pole at 1, since the sum of the differences between each summand and its integral on [n,n+1] converges locally uniformly there. If any nonprincipal L-function vanished at 1, the product over all h=φ(K) characters would therefore be holomorphic throughout Re s>0. For Re s>1, its Euler factor at p∤K is (1−p^(−rs))^(−h/r), where r is the order of p in the unit group. Indeed, character values at p run through the r-th roots of unity equally often, as follows by summing their powers by character orthogonality. Thus the product has a Dirichlet series with nonnegative coefficients and coefficient at least 1 at every n^h with gcd(n,K)=1. In the Taylor series at s=2 evaluated at s=1/h, termwise differentiation of the Dirichlet series gives nonnegative terms. Interchanging the sums shows that the Taylor sum equals the Dirichlet series evaluated at 1/h. The Taylor series converges because 2−1/h<2, whereas the Dirichlet series dominates the divergent sum of 1/n over n coprime to K. This contradiction proves the required nonvanishing at 1.

Consequently D_K(1+z)=1/(φ(K)z)+B_K+O(z), where B_K is the average of the differences of the regular logarithmic derivatives. This constant is real because D_K is real for real s>1 by its Dirichlet series. The definition gives C_{d,K}=B_K−1/φ(K), so both poles in F_K cancel and F_K extends holomorphically to a neighborhood of 0.
